Auto Ontology
Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own.
It enables developers to:
Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs.
Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems.
Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.
Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API.
Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question.
Benchmarks
To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the
ontology SQL evaluation repository.

Key Features
**Natural-language querying** of structured data — questions are translated to
SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM.
**Semantic catalog / ontology layer** over relational sources, stored in
Postgres alongside the catalog it describes.
**Authentication & RBAC** —using Better Auth.
**Web UI** for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings.
**Flexible deployment** — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a
local stack.
Software Components
| Component | Technology | Role | Default port |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------ |
| Frontend | Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma | Web UI, authentication, API gateway | 3000 |
| Backend | FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain | Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs | 3001 |
| Ingestion worker | FastAPI (Python 3.12+) | Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings | 3002 |
| Postgres + pgvector | Relational Database | App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store | 5432 |
| HashiCorp Vault | Optional | Secure storage of connection credentials | — |
NVIDIA NIM
Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted
NVIDIA API catalog (integrate.api.nvidia.com) or
self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in .env.example are:
**LLM:** nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b
**Embeddings:** nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b
**Reranking:** nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2
The endpoints and models are configured via the DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT, DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL,
EMBED_ENDPOINT, and EMBED_MODEL environment variables and require a
DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY.
Model triplets
Each model role is configured by a **triplet** of environment variables —
_ENDPOINT (URL), _API_KEY, and _MODEL:
| Prefix | Role |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| DEFAULT_MODELS | Shared default; every field below falls back to it. |
| REASONING | Main chat / NL-to-SQL model. |
| NON_REASONING | Lighter model used for entity extraction. |
| EMBED | Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query). |
| RERANK | Reranker used by the retrieval flow. |
You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field
left unset falls back to the matching DEFAULT_MODELS_. So the simplest
setup is to fill in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and override per-triplet fields only where
they differ (e.g. EMBED_MODEL, NON_REASONING_MODEL). *_API_KEY also falls
back to the legacy NVIDIA_API_KEY for backward compatibility.

Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
uv, and an NVIDIA API key (nvapi-...) from

Skills For Real Engineers
![skills.sh](https://skills.sh/mattpocock/skills)
My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding.
Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve.
These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. They work with any model. They're based on decades of engineering experience. Hack around with them. Make them your own. Enjoy.
If you want to keep up with changes to these skills, and any new ones I create, you can join ~60,000 other devs on my newsletter:
Sign Up To The Newsletter
Installation (30-second setup)
A plugin updates itself. skills.sh copies editable files into your project, and you update them by hand. Pick one per agent, because installing both gives you every skill twice.
1. Get the skills
Claude Code
claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official
Updates itself by default.
Codex
codex plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
codex plugin add mattpocock-skills@mattpocock
Updates itself at startup.
GitHub Copilot (CLI and VS Code)
copilot plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
copilot plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock
Then, once, add to ~/.copilot/settings.json:
{
"extraKnownMarketplaces": {
"mattpocock": { "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "mattpocock/skills" }, "autoUpdate": true }
}
}
In VS Code, run **Chat: Install Plugin From Source** and enter https://github.com/mattpocock/skills. It updates daily.
Gemini CLI (manual updates)
gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/engineering
gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/productivity
Re-run both commands to update.
Any other agent, or editable files (manual updates)
npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills -a # cursor, opencode, devin, windsurf, amp, pi; omit -a to choose
When the installer asks which skills to take, include setup-matt-pocock-skills. To update, run npx skills@latest update, and re-run add to pick up new skills.
2. Run /setup-matt-pocock-skills
In your agent, run it once per repo. It will:
Ask you which issue tracker you want to use (GitHub, GitLab, local files, or anything else you describe)
Ask you what labels you apply to tickets when you triage them (/triage uses labels)
Ask you where you want to save any docs we create
3. Bam - you're ready to go.
Why These Skills Exist
I built these skills as a way to fix common failure modes I see with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents.
#1: The Agent Didn't Do What I Want
> "No-one knows exactly what they want"
>
> David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer
*The Problem**. The most common failure mode in software development is misalignment. You think the dev knows what you want. Then you see what they've built - and you realize it didn't understand you at all.
This is just the same in the AI age. There is a communication gap between you and the agent. The fix for this is a **grilling session** - getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building.
*The Fix** is to use:
/grill-me - for non-code uses
/grill-with-docs - same as /grill-me, but adds more goodies (see below)
These are my most popular skills. They help you align with the agent before you get started, and think deeply about the change you're making. Use them _every_ time you want to make a change.
#2: The Agent Is Way Too Verbose
> With a ubiquitous language, conversations among developers and expressions of the code are all derived from the same domain model.
>
> Eric Evans, Domain-Driven-Design
*The Problem**: At the start of a project, devs and the people they're building the software for (the domain experts) are usually speaking different languages.
I felt the same tension with my agents. Agents are usually dropped into a project and asked to figure out the jargon as they go. So they use 20 words where 1 will do.
*The Fix** for this is a shared language. It's a document that helps agents decode the jargon used in the project.
Example
Here's an example glossary (still named CONTEXT.md at that pinned commit, from before the skills renamed the convention), from my course-video-manager repo. Which one is easier to read?
**BEFORE**: "There's a problem when a lesson inside a section of a course is made 'real' (i.e. given a spot in the file system)"
**AFTER**: "There's a problem with the materialization cascade"
This concision pays off session after session.
This is built into /grill-with-docs. It's a grilling session, but that helps you build a shared language with the AI, and document hard-to-explain decisions in ADR's.
It's hard to explain how powerful this is. It might be the single coolest technique in this repo. Try it, and see.
> [!TIP]
> A shared language has many other benefits than reducing verbosity:
>
> - **Variables, functions and files are named consistently**, using the shared language
> - As a result, the **codebase is easier to navigate** for the agent
> - The agent also **spends fewer tokens on thinking**, because it has access to a more concise language
#3: The Code Doesn't Work
> "Always take small, deliberate steps. The rate of feedback is your speed limit. Never take on a task that’s too big."
>
> David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer
*The Problem**: Let's say that you and the agent are aligned on what to build. What happens when the agent _still_ produces crap?
It's time to look at your feedback loops. Without feedback on how the code it produces actually runs, the agent will be flying blind.
*The Fix**: You need the usual tranche of feedback loops: static types, browser access, and automated tests.
For automated tests, a red-green-refactor loop is critical. This is where the agent writes a failing test first, then fixes the test. This helps give the agent a consistent level of feedback that results in far better code.

What is Floci?
Floci is a free, open-source local AWS emulator for development, testing, and CI.
It gives you AWS-shaped services on your machine without requiring a cloud account, an auth token, or paid feature gates. Point your AWS SDK, CLI, Terraform, CDK, OpenTofu, or test suite at http://localhost:4566 and keep your existing workflows.
Already using LocalStack? Floci is a drop-in replacement: swap the image and keep going. See Migrating from LocalStack.
Floci is the AWS member of the Floci emulator family, named after floccus, the cloud formation that looks like popcorn.
| Emulator | Cloud | Port |
|---|---|:---:|
| **floci** | **AWS** | **4566** |
| floci-az | Azure | 4577 |
| floci-gcp | GCP | 4588 |
| floci-oci | OCI | 4599 |
Quick Start
The fastest way to run Floci is with the official CLI
floci start
No Docker? Each release also ships a standalone floci-aws
binary for Linux, macOS and Windows; see Native binary.
Export the AWS environment variables:
eval $(floci env)
Use your existing AWS tools normally:
aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket
aws dynamodb create-table \n-table-name demo-table \n-attribute-definitions AttributeName=pk,AttributeType=S \n-key-schema AttributeName=pk,KeyType=HASH \n-billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST
aws dynamodb list-tables
Watch it run
This short demo shows the CLI flow: start Floci, export the local AWS environment, run standard AWS CLI commands, and stop the emulator.
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b55714dc-ef36-40ae-a734-cd2cadc288a8
All AWS services are available at http://localhost:4566. Any published AWS region works, in every partition. Credentials can be any non-empty values unless you explicitly enable stricter service-specific auth checks.
Prefer Docker Compose?
Create a compose.yaml file:
services:
floci:
image: floci/floci:latest
ports:
"4566:4566"
Start Floci:
docker compose up
Then configure your AWS environment manually:
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test
Using the old hectorvent/floci image?
Update your image name:
Before
image: hectorvent/floci:latest
After
image: floci/floci:latest
The old hectorvent/floci repository no longer receives updates.
Web Console
Floci ships a browser console for inspecting the resources in your local emulator.
*Open it at:** http://localhost:4566/_floci/ui
Nothing runs at boot. The first request pulls the console image, starts it as a sidecar container on Floci's Docker network, hands it Floci's own reachable address plus the standard AWS environment, polls its health endpoint, and redirects the browser once it reports it can reach Floci. The sidecar's port is bound by Docker, so it needs no ports: entry of your own, and its logs are streamed into CloudWatch Logs under /floci/ui.
Starting a container needs the Docker socket:
services:
floci:
image: floci/floci:latest
ports:
"4566:4566"
volumes:
/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_ENABLED | true | Enable the console sidecar |
| FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_IMAGE | floci/floci-ui:0.7.0 | Console image to run |
| FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_CONTAINER_NAME | floci-ui | Name of the sidecar container |
| FLOCI_SERVICES_UI_PORT | 4500 | Host port the console is published on |

Claude-Mem seamlessly preserves context across sessions by automatically capturing tool usage observations, generating semantic summaries, and making them available to future sessions. This enables Claude to maintain continuity of knowledge about projects even after sessions end or reconnect.
--
Quick Start
Install claude-mem for Grok Bot:
npx claude-mem install --ide grok-bot
Grok Bot has no host hooks, so we watch the chat log files. Default is CMEM Pro, the hosted memory. Local observer is opt-in: --provider host. Installing this plugin does not install Cursor.
*Awareness push pilot (LFG + Orifice):** needle observations (decision, bugfix, security_alert, sensitive) are appended as dated - YYYY-MM-DD [awareness] … lines into that bot's memory/log/YYYY-MM.md. Grok Bot already re-reads the log from disk. This does not write profile.md, user-memory, or project memory. Disable with CLAUDE_MEM_GROK_BOT_AWARENESS_ENABLED=false.
Install with a single command:
npx claude-mem install
The installer sets everything up first, then asks you to sign in to claude-mem in your browser (email magic link — no card required). Signing in provisions a memory key for your account and unlocks the **claude-mem observer** with a **30 Day Free Trial**: memory runs off-plan, so you get up to 100% more usage from your plan. When the free trial ends, memory automatically falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe. After sign-in you pick your memory provider — the claude-mem observer, your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan.
Prefer to skip the sign-in? Pass an explicit --provider flag, set CLAUDE_MEM_ONLINE_OPTIN=false, or run in CI/non-interactive shells — the installer completes without any account interaction.
Or install for OpenCode:
npx claude-mem install --ide opencode
This works with OpenCode 1.3.4 or later, including OpenCode 2. Restart OpenCode after installing.
Or install for **T3 Code** (Codex and Claude Code providers):
npx claude-mem install --ide t3code
The installer discovers T3 Code's enabled providers, registers native Claude-Mem plugins in their configured homes, and supports T3-managed Codex. Restart T3 Code, trust the provider's hooks when prompted, and start a new thread. See the T3 Code integration guide for custom server settings, status, and removal.

agent-desktop
Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree.
agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library.
Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output, and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads.
Install
npm install -g agent-desktop
agent-desktop status # platform, permissions, supported surfaces
agent-desktop permissions --guide # macOS: walks you through the Accessibility grant
Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64.
For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from
GitHub Releases and keep its helper beside the executable.
On macOS and Linux, Homebrew also works: brew install agent-desktop. There is no official Scoop package yet.
The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket.
Release archives and building from source are covered in Installation.
Quick start
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # observe again to verify
Each command prints one JSON envelope. A trimmed snapshot:
{
"version": "2.6",
"ok": true,
"command": "snapshot",
"data": {
"app": "Finder",
"snapshot_id": "s8f3k2p9",
"ref_count": 59,
"complete": true,
"tree": {
"role": "window",
"name": "Downloads",
"children": [
{ "role": "treeitem", "name": "Documents", "ref_id": "@s8f3k2p9:e8", "available_actions": ["Click"] }
]
}
}
}
**Refs belong to their snapshot.** A bare @e8 is rejected with INVALID_ARGS. When the UI changes, an action
returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET: take a new snapshot and use its refs.
**Several windows** give AMBIGUOUS_TARGET; snapshot lists the candidate window ids in error.details. Pass one
with --window-id.
**Dense apps:** map first with snapshot --skeleton --app Slack -i --compact, then drill into one region with
snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e3 -i --compact.
**Headless by default.** Ref actions use the accessibility API without moving the pointer or taking focus. The global
-headed flag allows physical input.
**Post-action waits** observe the ref's original process. Window-owned refs stay pinned to their original window,
including refs captured from a sheet, alert, popover, focused view, or Linux menu. macOS application menus keep
their application-owned surface and need no document window. The wait reads the whole pinned window, so overlay
selectors share its scope. Wait scope and results
describe the selector limits.
type, set-value, and clipboard-set accept --stdin for piped text, keeping it out of process arguments. Run secret steps as separate commands; batch JSON text appears in process arguments.
**PowerShell.** Quote every ref ('@s8f3k2p9:e8'), because a bare @token is the splatting operator.
The full walkthrough is in the quick start.
How it works
Your agent calls the CLI, or the C library in process. Both run the same core, which reaches the OS only through PlatformAdapter. Each binary is built for one OS and talks to that OS's accessibility API.
For AI agents
The binary carries guides that match its version:
agent-desktop skills get desktop # the loop, refs, verification and retry rules
agent-desktop skills get platform # what differs on the OS you run on
agent-desktop --help # flags for one command
Install the skill into an agent harness from skills.sh:
npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop
Or add this to your AGENTS.md:
Use agent-desktop to see and operate desktop apps. Before the first use, run
agent-desktop skills get desktop and agent-desktop skills get platform, and follow them.
Retry a failed command only when error.disposition.retry is safe. See JSON output for the envelope, error codes, and exit codes.
MCP
agent-desktop mcp serves every command as an MCP tool over stdio. A tool is named after its command (desktop_snapshot, desktop_click, desktop_session_start), takes that command's arguments, and returns its JSON envelope:
{ "mcpServers": { "agent-desktop": { "command": "agent-desktop", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
Global flags given to mcp, such as --session, --headed or --trace, apply to every call.
Commands
agent-desktop has 60 command names, 56 operational commands. The other four (key-down, key-up, mouse-down, mouse-up) refuse to run until a daemon can release a held key or button. Commands documents each one.
| Group | Commands |
|---|---|
| Observe | snapshot, find, get, is, screenshot, list-surfaces |
| Act on a ref | click, double-click, triple-click, right-click, type, set-value, clear, focus, select, toggle, check, uncheck, expand, collapse, scroll, scroll-to |
| Keyboard and mouse | press, hover, drag, mouse-move, mouse-click, mouse-wheel, key-down, key-up, mouse-down, mouse-up |
| Apps and windows | launch, close-app, list-apps, list-windows, list-displays, focus-window, resize-window, move-window, minimize, maximize, restore, open-system-surface |

🌱 Spec Kit
Build with a spec, fix a bug, or assess an idea — with your coding agent.
English ·
简体中文 ·
日本語 ·
한국어
Spec Kit is an open source toolkit that gives AI coding agents structured
processes, reusable templates, and documented outcomes. Start with a ready-made
process, customize it, or bring your own.
Choose your process
| What you need | Process | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build a feature or application | Spec-Driven Development | A specification carried through planning, implementation, and convergence |
| Diagnose and repair broken behavior | Bug fixing | An assessed cause, scoped fix, and recorded verification |
| Decide whether an idea deserves investment | Idea assessment | An evidence-backed go, clarify, or stop decision |
| Adopt or create a different process | Your own process | A process adapted or assembled from reusable primitives |
These are independent entry points, not mandatory phases. SDD ships in core;
bug fixing and assessment are bundled extensions you install when needed, and
the primitives below let you adopt or create other processes.
Capabilities
Spec Kit combines ready-to-use processes with composable mechanisms:
| Capability | Spec Kit mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Connect to or switch between coding agents | Integration |
| Add a command, quality gate, or complete process | Extension |
| Connect a process to an external tool or service | Extension |
| React to coding-agent lifecycle events | Extension runtime event |
| Run extension commands before or after Spec Kit commands | Extension hook |
| Adapt templates, commands, terminology, or methodology | Preset |
| Enforce organizational or regulatory standards | Preset |
| Override a template for one project | Project-local override |
| Automate prompts, commands, gates, and shell tasks | Workflow |
| Modify an installed workflow without forking it | Workflow overlay |
| Add reusable executable behavior to workflows | Workflow step |
| Install a curated setup for a role or team | Bundle |
| Discover community components | Catalog |
| Host a private catalog of approved components | Catalog |
| Access private catalogs and component downloads | Authentication |
| Work offline or behind a firewall | Local sources and self-hosted catalogs |
| Inspect which layer supplies a command, template, or script | Artifact inventory |
Search the active catalogs with commands such as specify extension search,
specify preset search, specify workflow search, and specify bundle search.
Spec Kit includes community catalogs, and organizations can add their own
curated sources. Catalog listings are not audits or endorsements, so review
community source code before installing or running it.
Get started
You need Python 3.11+, uv,
and a supported AI coding agent on Linux, macOS, or Windows.
Run these commands in your terminal to install Spec Kit and create a project.
This example uses GitHub Copilot.
uv tool install specify-cli
specify init my-project --integration copilot
cd my-project
After installing the Specify CLI and creating your project, launch your coding
agent in the project directory, then choose a process below.
For other setups:
Installation for pinned releases, other installers, CI, and troubleshooting.
Existing projects to start with code you already have.
Other agents for integration keys and invocation syntax.
Upgrade to update an existing installation.
Spec-Driven Development
Define what to build and why, then turn the specification into a plan, tasks,
and working code.
The minimal flow is shown below. Create a constitution once per project and
repeat the remaining steps for each feature. Run these skills in your agent's
chat, not your terminal, one at a time, reviewing each result before continuing.
This example uses GitHub Copilot's default skills syntax. For another agent,
use its equivalent invocation syntax.
/speckit-constitution Create principles focused on code quality, testing, and maintainability.
/speckit-specify Build a photo organizer with albums grouped by date and a tile preview of each album.
/speckit-plan Use Vite with vanilla JavaScript. Keep images local and store metadata in SQLite.
/speckit-tasks
/speckit-implement
/speckit-converge
Repeat implement and converge until convergence reports Converged.
For clarification, checklists, and consistency analysis, see the SDD walkthrough.

gstack
gstack turns Claude Code (and other coding agents) into a virtual engineering team: a CEO who rethinks the product, an eng manager who locks architecture, a designer who catches AI slop, a reviewer who finds production bugs, a QA lead who opens a real browser, a security officer who runs OWASP + STRIDE audits, and a release engineer who ships the PR. All slash commands, all Markdown, all free, MIT license.
I'm Garry Tan, President & CEO of Y Combinator. This is the open source software factory I use every day, and I'm sharing it because these tools should be available to everyone. The story, the productivity numbers and how I run ten sprints at once are in Why gstack.
Fork it. Improve it. Make it yours. And if you want to hate on free open source software — you're welcome to, but I'd rather you just try it first.
*Who this is for:**
**Founders and CEOs** — especially technical ones who still want to ship
**First-time Claude Code users** — structured roles instead of a blank prompt
**Tech leads and staff engineers** — rigorous review, QA, and release automation on every PR
Quick start
1. Install gstack (two pastes, about 30 seconds of setup; see below).
2. Run /office-hours and describe what you're building. It pushes back on your framing and writes a design doc the other skills read.
3. Run /review on any branch with changes. It finds the bugs that pass CI but break in production, and fixes the obvious ones.
4. Run /qa on your staging URL, or on an isolated local API, CLI, job or webhook. It opens a real browser, reproduces bugs and fixes them.
Stop there. You'll know if this is for you. When you want the whole sprint, /autoplan reviews a plan end to end and /ship runs tests, review and the PR.
Install — about 30 seconds
*Requirements:** Claude Code, Git, Bun v1.4.2+ (the tested version; setup refuses Bun older than 1.3.3, which would let compiled tools read a project's .env), and Node.js on Windows. **Recommended on macOS:** the Aside browser (macOS 15+), which the browser skills, /make-pdf and /diagram drive first with your real logged-in sessions; without it, ./setup builds gstack's own bundled browser. /cso needs a native toolchain as well; setup says so and leaves it unavailable when the toolchain is absent. Timing, the /cso prerequisites and the hooks setup registers: docs/install.md.
Step 1: Install on your machine
Open Claude Code and paste this. Claude does the rest.
> Install gstack: run **git clone --single-branch --depth 1 https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git ~/.claude/skills/gstack && cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack && ./setup** then add a "gstack" section to CLAUDE.md that says to use the /browse skill from gstack for all web browsing and never use mcp\_\_claude-in-chrome\_\_\* tools. Claude Code lists the installed skills itself, so the section needs no skill list. Then ask the user if they also want to add gstack to the current project so teammates get it.
Step 2: Team mode — auto-update for shared repos (recommended)
From inside your repo, paste this. Switches you to team mode, bootstraps the repo so teammates get gstack automatically, and commits the change:
(cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack && ./setup --team) && ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-team-init required && git add .claude/ CLAUDE.md && git commit -m "require gstack for AI-assisted work"
No vendored files in your repo, no version drift, no manual upgrades. Every Claude Code session starts with a fast auto-update check (throttled to once/hour, network-failure-safe, completely silent). Team mode follows the stable channel: the twice-weekly tagged release (Monday and Thursday, at most once every 72 hours, plus verified security and regression fixes), not every merge to main. gstack-config set update_channel main follows every merge instead; see docs/releases.md.
Swap required for optional if you'd rather nudge teammates than block them.
Team mode's required hook runs on Node.js, so every teammate needs Node.js on PATH (details). To remove gstack later: docs/uninstall.md.
Other AI Agents
gstack runs on more agents than Claude. Bare ./setup installs for Claude
Code only (run inside OpenClaw, Hermes or a Dot, it also registers gstack's
skills with that harness: docs/hosts.md).
Pick another agent with --host , or install for every agent setup
detects on this machine with --host auto:
git clone --single-branch --depth 1 https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git ~/gstack
cd ~/gstack && ./setup --host auto # or: ./setup --host codex
./setup --status # one row per install: host, tier, scope, version, path
An explicit --host X installs for X only and never changes another agent's
install. /gstack-upgrade refreshes every install it registered, one row per
host, and says which ones failed.
Tiers: **full** is certified by a real workflow run (see
Certify your host); **experimental**
installs and passes the conformance tests but has no certification run yet;
*instruction-only** installs nothing: setup prints what to copy.
| Agent | Tier | Install | First invocation | Safety skills | Outside review needs | Repair |
|-------|------|---------|------------------|---------------|----------------------|--------|
| Claude Code | full | --host claude (default) | /office-hours | enforced (hooks block) | Codex CLI, signed in | ./setup --host claude |
| OpenAI Codex CLI | experimental | --host codex → ${CODEX_HOME:-~/.codex}/skills/gstack-*/ | ask for gstack-office-hours | advisory, not blocked | Claude Code CLI, signed in | ./setup --host codex |

| Cursor | experimental | --host cursor → ~/.cursor/skills/gstack-*/ | ask for gstack-office-hours | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | ./setup --host cursor |
| Factory Droid | experimental | --host factory → ~/.factory/skills/gstack-*/ | ask for gstack-office-hours | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | ./setup --host factory |
| Kiro | experimental | --host kiro → ~/.kiro/skills/gstack-*/ | ask for gstack-office-hours | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | ./setup --host kiro |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | experimental | --host copilot → ~/.copilot/skills/gstack-*/ | /gstack-office-hours | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | ./setup --host copilot |
| Antigravity CLI | experimental | --host agy (or --host antigravity) → ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills/gstack-*/ | /gstack-office-hours | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | ./setup --host agy |
| Gemini CLI | experimental | --host gemini (or --host gemini-cli) → ~/.gemini/skills/gstack-*/ | ask for gstack-office-hours | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | ./setup --host gemini |
| Slate | instruction-only | --host slate (points at the Claude install; Slate reads .claude/skills) | /office-hours via the Claude install | advisory, not blocked | — | ./setup --host claude |
| OpenClaw | experimental | --host openclaw (five task skills and one gstack router skill in OpenClaw's skills folder; automatic when setup runs inside OpenClaw; ACP route in docs/OPENCLAW.md) | ask for the task; the agent opens the matching task skill or the gstack router | advisory, not blocked | — | ./setup --host openclaw |

| GBrain (mod) | instruction-only | --host gbrain (brain-aware variants ship from the GBrain repo) | — | advisory, not blocked | — | — |
Per-host notes (agent harnesses, Copilot, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw and ClawHub, the Codex behavioral profile and model tiers, outside-review providers, the design binary's models) are in docs/hosts.md. Any rules-reading agent (Zed, Amp, Jules) can use the 2KB agents digest with no install. Adding a host: docs/ADDING_A_HOST.md.
See it work
You: I want to build a daily briefing app for my calendar.
You: /office-hours
Claude: [asks about the pain — specific examples, not hypotheticals]
You: Multiple Google calendars, events with stale info, wrong locations.
Prep takes forever and the results aren't good enough...
Claude: I'm going to push back on the framing. You said "daily briefing
app." But what you actually described is a personal chief of
staff AI.
[extracts 5 capabilities you didn't realize you were describing]
[challenges 4 premises — you agree, disagree, or adjust]
[generates 3 implementation approaches with effort estimates]
RECOMMENDATION: Ship the narrowest wedge tomorrow, learn from
real usage. The full vision is a 3-month project — start with
the daily briefing that actually works.
[writes design doc → feeds into downstream skills automatically]
You: /plan-ceo-review
[reads the design doc, challenges scope, runs 10-section review]
You: /plan-eng-review
[ASCII diagrams for data flow, state machines, error paths]
[test matrix, failure modes, security concerns]
You: Approve plan. Exit plan mode.
[writes 2,400 lines across 11 files. ~8 minutes.]

Same short prompt at every size, and the output is byte-identical from the smallest machine to the largest; only the clock changes. One machine, 124 cores, fast NVMe drive: the first three rows still read the model from disk each step, so a slower drive is slower there, while the 128 GB+ row keeps everything in memory and no longer waits on the disk. On that same machine v1.0.0 made the math per token about 8× lighter, a follow-up question in a chat 3.9× faster, and long prompts about half as costly. (A token is roughly a short word-piece; the two runnable demos below are the original captures on a slower drive, so their clock reads a little higher.) Full data in docs/data/.

batch command deliberately asks for a raw continuation. The official Kimi K3 checkpoint
is also chat-capable; use the XTML REPL below when you want answers and multi-turn history.
Give the same batch request more memory and the answer does not change, only the clock:

docs/data/.
The dense trunk stays in memory to whatever depth you choose and streams the rest; the
1.45 TB of routed experts are never resident, and are multiplied straight out of their
packed 4-bit form. The consequence is that **the same model runs in 8 GB and in 224 GB and
produces byte-identical output at every budget between.**

Disc Image Studio 是一个多平台的光盘盘的文字成与刻录工具，帮助您使用任何刻录光驱在任何 DVD / CD / 单层蓝光光盘上刻蚀出肉眼可见的ภาพ。

## 概述
Disc Image Studio อัลบั้มภาพ转换成符合 CD、DVD 与单层 BD-R ข้อมูลเพิ่มเติม

## 快速开始
Windows สำหรับ win-x64.exe 后可直接运行。Linux 或 macOS 请下载与 CPU 匹配的实验性 CLI 压缩包，解压后运行 ./disc-image-studio --help。这些发布包均自带 .NET 运行时。 GitHub Releases

## 1. 新建工程
在主页选择 CD、DVD 或蓝光，指定输出位置后创建工程。

## 2. 设计盘面
伽马、亮度与灰阶档位伽马、亮度与灰阶档位。

## 3. 预览与导出
在预览页核对盘的投影，在导出页生成 ISO / RAW / WAV+CUE，或使用即时刻录功能直接写入空白盘的。

## 3. 预览与导出
即时刻录为实验性功能，请只使用可报废的测试介质。

## 光盘数据生成
- ซีดี：支持任何 ซีดี 。您可导出带格式头的 WAV 音轨及配套 CUE, 兼容 cdrecord, ImgBurn 等刻录软件;也允许导出 RAW 音轨。详见 CD 刻录兼容说明。 - DVD 支持：支持任何 DVD。您可导出 ISO 镜出。 - ข้อมูลเพิ่มเติม: BD-R 25 GB，支持纯绘与 UDF 2.01 文件。详见 ADDINGBLURAY.md。 -随盘文件：CD／DVD／蓝光可在设计页直接选择要保存的文件

## 辅助标定
ดิสก์อิมเมจสตูดิโอ提供粗标定、边界标定和精细标定流程，通过盘的的外半径与轨距分布。下เลดี้的历史实盘对比中，校准前采用恒定轨距，十字线的径向线条出现明显弯曲;使用辅助标定得到的三次轨距参数重新生成并刻录后，线条更接近径向直线。实ข้อมูลเพิ่มเติม

## 辅助标定
第一次使用可跟随DVD 标定实操教程：คำต่อคำ AZO DVD-R，查看三个标定阶段的实际取点、参数变化与参考值，以及精标后的盘เลดี้效果。完整流程与参数说明见辅助标定说明。

## 刻录
- 镜本文件输出：您可以导出完整 ISO / RAW 文件并使用合适的刻录软件手动刻录。 -即时流式刻录（实验性）：CD、DVD 与 BD-R 边生成边刻录，不保存完整镜;BD-R 走 MMC 顺序写入。

Disc Image Studio 是一个多平台的光盘盘面图像生成与刻录工具，帮助您使用任何刻录光驱在任何 DVD / CD / 单层蓝光 光盘上刻蚀出肉眼可见的图像。

概述
Disc Image Studio 可将一张图片转换成符合 CD、DVD 与单层 BD-R 光盘物理层约束的数据，刻录后将使光盘盘面呈现肉眼可见的图案。
界面预览
--
快速开始
Windows 下载 win-x64.exe 后可直接运行。Linux 或 macOS 请下载与 CPU 匹配的**实验性 CLI** 压缩包，解压后运行 ./disc-image-studio --help。这些发布包均自带 .NET 运行时。 GitHub Releases
1. 新建工程
在主页选择 CD、DVD 或蓝光，指定输出位置后创建工程。
2. 设计盘面
在设计页导入图片，用图层完成排版，并在右栏「影调」模块调整抖动、伽马、亮度与灰阶档位。
3. 预览与导出
在预览页核对盘面投影，在导出页生成 ISO / RAW / WAV+CUE，或使用即时刻录功能直接写入空白盘片。
即时刻录为实验性功能，请只使用可报废的测试介质。
功能
光盘数据生成
**CD 支持**：支持任何 CD 。您可导出带格式头的 WAV 音轨及配套 CUE，兼容 cdrecord, ImgBurn等刻录软件；也允许导出 RAW 音轨。详见 CD 刻录兼容说明。
**DVD 支持**：支持任何 DVD。您可导出 ISO 镜像。
**蓝光支持**：支持任何单层 BD-R 25 GB，支持纯绘图与 UDF 2.01 文件。详见 ADDING_BLURAY.md。
**随盘文件**：CD／DVD／蓝光可在设计页直接选择要保存的文件夹及内圈／外圈位置，也可在导出页调整；设置随工程保存。
**文件区域预览**：混合盘的设计投影和成品读回用黄色标出文件区（含文件系统）。
**介质灰度方案**：CD 与 DVD 均使用黑白二阶，CD 使用 0D / AA，DVD 扰码域使用 A5 / 92。详见 PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md。
**灰度抖动工具**：独立程序也可将原图处理为 0/255 黑白二阶 PNG；支持打开或拖入原图、并排预览及无损 PNG 导出。详见使用与构建说明。
**盘片预设**：内置数个品牌的光盘参数，覆盖 CD／DVD／BD。您也可将自己标定好的数据贡献给我们，详见预设维护说明。
辅助标定
Disc Image Studio 提供粗标定、边界标定和精细标定流程，通过盘面照片估计内外半径与轨距分布。下面的历史实盘对比中，校准前采用恒定轨距，十字线的径向线条出现明显弯曲；使用辅助标定得到的三次轨距参数重新生成并刻录后，线条更接近径向直线。实测精度取决于照片矫正、取点和复刻验证，参数保存的小数位数不代表测量精度。
| 校准前 · 恒定轨距 | 校准后 · 三次轨距 |
| --- | --- |
| !校准前的 DVD 实拍：径向十字线明显弯曲 | !校准后的 DVD 实拍：径向十字线更接近直线 |
| P20261004-133519.jpg | P20261004-135416.jpg |
第一次使用可跟随DVD 标定实操教程：Verbatim AZO DVD-R，查看照片矫正、三个标定阶段的实际取点、参数变化与参考值，以及精标后的盘面效果。完整流程与参数说明见辅助标定说明。
刻录
**镜像文件输出**：您可以导出完整 ISO / RAW 文件并使用合适的刻录软件手动刻录。
**即时流式刻录（实验性）**：CD、DVD 与 BD-R 边生成边刻录，不保存完整镜像；BD-R 走 MMC 顺序写入。
**不要使用非空白介质！**
系统与设备要求
桌面版需要 Windows 10 2004（2004/20H1，19041）及以上，或 Windows 11。
构建：.NET 10 SDK（global.json 锁定 10.0.x）；自行构建的非自包含 GUI 需要 .NET 10 Windows 桌面运行时。Release EXE 已包含运行时，无需另行安装 .NET。
“即时刻录”功能需要一台 Windows 可识别的 CD / DVD / BD 刻录机与空白盘片；BD-R 需要支持顺序写入的单层空白盘。
构建与运行
dotnet build DiscImageStudio.slnx --configuration Release
dotnet run --project src/DiscImageStudio.App --configuration Release
构建回归检查：
dotnet run --project src/DvdImageSolver --configuration Release -- selftest
dotnet run --project tests/DiscImageStudio.ArchitectureTests --configuration Release
版本规则、CI 生成 EXE、Release 草稿检查、MSIX 打包与签名流程见发布指南。
命令行
Linux（glibc）可选 linux-x64 或 linux-arm64。Apple Silicon Mac 选 osx-arm64，Intel Mac 选 osx-x64。CLI 在本地生成镜像，实际写盘可交给支持相应镜像或音轨的刻录软件。
使用 .NET 10 SDK 从源码运行 CLI
dotnet run --project src/DiscImageStudio.Cli -c Release -- --help
CLI 可读取 PNG、JPEG、BMP 和 GIF，使用动画图片的第一帧。下面的例子用两扇区音轨验证安装，同时生成配套 CUE。
./disc-image-studio cd-generate --input picture.png --output sample.wav --sectors 2
| 命令 | 说明 |
| --- | --- |
| solve | 使用固定快速纹理映射（CW 方向）生成 DVD 镜像，黑白纹理可选抖动混合 |
| encode | 将单个 DVD ECC 块编码为 NRZI 通道电平 |
| calibrate | 标定投影：按生成几何从 DVD 源图片取样，按实测几何投到盘面 |
| simulate | 按实测半径对生成的 DVD ISO 做读回模拟 |
| selftest | 运行 DVD 引擎的确定性回归自检 |
| cd-generate | 无随盘文件时生成 WAV + CUE / RAW 音轨；指定 --data-dir 时生成 CD 数据盘 ISO |
| cd-preview-warp | 标定投影：按实测几何投影 CD 源图片 |
| cd-preview-track | 按标定几何渲染已有的 WAV 或 RAW CD-DA 音轨（读回模拟） |
| bd-generate | 生成完整 BD-R ISO，并写出 .json sidecar |
| bd-info / bd-probe / bd-encode | 导出 BD 参数、原始负载探针或单个 ECC 簇诊断 |
各命令的完整参数见对应文档。
源码结构
src/DiscImageStudio.Cli/ Linux 和 macOS 离线命令行入口
src/DiscImageStudio.ImageIO/ WIC 和跨平台图像编解码
src/DiscImageStudio.Core/ 介质无关的模块契约、工程/预设模型、任务与命令目录
src/DiscImageStudio.Imaging/ CD/DVD/BD 共用的图片预处理与抖动辅助
src/DiscImageStudio.Burning/ Windows IMAPI2 设备枚举、流缓冲与安全刻录层
src/DiscImageStudio.Cd/ CD-DA 生成核心与 CD 模块
src/DiscImageStudio.Dvd/ DVD 引擎适配模块
src/DiscImageStudio.BluRay/ BD-R 几何、17PP/ECC、3T/6T 映射、流式生成与 ISO

Scrapling is a Python Web Scraping framework that brings fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, powerful parsing, and concurrent crawling into one library.
Scrape static pages, render JavaScript, interact with websites, and extract data from the API calls behind them. Build crawlers with reusable sessions, proxy rotation, automatic retries, pause/resume, and built-in data exports.
Use it from Python, the terminal, or your AI agent through its MCP server and Agent Skill. From extracting a few fields to collecting a whole website as clean Markdown, Scrapling covers the full scraping workflow.
What you can do with Scrapling
**Fetch & interact**: Fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, JavaScript rendering, Cloudflare Turnstile/Interstitial handling, persistent sessions, and background API capture.
**Parse & extract**: CSS, XPath, text and regex search, adaptive element tracking, similar-element matching, and clean Markdown output.
**Crawl & export**: Concurrent spiders, proxy rotation, retries, AutoThrottle, pause/resume, streaming, ready-made templates, and JSON/JSONL/CSV/XML exports.
**Scrape with AI or from your terminal**: An MCP server for AI agents to browse and extract data, an Agent Skill, CLI commands, and an interactive shell.
Start with a single page:
from scrapling.fetchers import Fetcher
page = Fetcher.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/')
quotes = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall()
print(quotes)
Or scale up with a spider:
from scrapling.spiders import Spider, Response
class QuotesSpider(Spider):
name = "quotes"
start_urls = ["https://quotes.toscrape.com/"]
async def parse(self, response: Response):
for quote in response.css('.quote'):
yield {
"text": quote.css('.text::text').get(),
"author": quote.css('.author::text').get(),
}
result = QuotesSpider().start()
print(len(result.items))
result.items.to_json("quotes.json")

🕷️ **Scrapy-like Spider API**: Define spiders with start_urls, async parse callbacks, and Request/Response objects.
⚡ **Concurrent Crawling**: Configurable concurrency limits, per-domain throttling, and download delays.

💾 **Pause & Resume**: Save pending requests and seen URLs with crawldir. Press Ctrl+C to stop gracefully and restart with the same directory.
📡 **Streaming Mode**: Stream scraped items as they arrive via async for item in spider.stream() with real-time stats - ideal for UI, pipelines, and long-running crawls.
🛡️ **Blocked Request Detection**: Automatic detection and retry of blocked requests with customizable logic.
